notes.meaning: Job begins his answer after Eliphaz finishes speaking. He refuses to accept his friends' accusations in silence and prepares to speak his mind once again. He wants to address their harsh charges directly.

Job tells his friends that he has heard these same arguments many times before. He calls them miserable comforters because their words only add grief instead of soothing his pain. Earthly advice often fails when a soul is in deep distress.

Job asks Eliphaz when his windy, empty speeches will finally stop. He questions what provokes his friends to keep arguing so harshly without listening to him. Words without sympathy do nothing to heal a hurting person.

Job notes that he could easily act the same way if their roles were reversed. He could mock them, shake his head in scorn, and pile on accusations while they sat in pain. It is easy to criticize others when we are comfortable and they are suffering.

Job says that if his friends were the ones suffering, he would choose to encourage them. He would speak gentle words to bring them relief instead of adding to their misery. True comfort aims to lift up those who are broken down.

Job explains that speaking out does not ease his inner torment, yet remaining silent does not help either. No matter what he does, his heavy sorrow stays with him. Deep grief can leave a person feeling completely trapped.

Job turns his lament to God, confessing that his strength is entirely exhausted. God has wiped out his household, taking away his children and leaving his home desolate. He feels crushed by the sudden loss of everyone he loved.

Job feels bound like a prisoner by his severe illness, which has left his body thin and wrinkled. His friends treat his wasting sickness as visible proof that he has sinned. Sickness and weakness can be wrongly judged by others as signs of guilt.

Job pictures his attacker as a fierce wild animal tearing him to pieces and glaring at him with burning anger. In his agony, he feels as though God Himself has become his enemy. Terrible pain can make a sufferer feel completely abandoned or attacked by God.

differ.view: Some Methodist commentators understand the fierce attacker described here as Satan rather than God.

notes.meaning: Job laments that people open their mouths wide to mock him and treat him with open contempt. Slapping the cheek was a severe insult in the ancient world, showing total disdain. This cruel mocking also foreshadows the rejection Jesus faced before His death.

Job recognizes that God has allowed unjust and wicked people to mistreat him. Whether he means desert raiders or his harsh friends, he knows his life is in their grasp by divine permission. It is painful to endure mistreatment when God seems to allow it.

Job remembers how peaceful and secure his life was before disasters struck without warning. He feels like a fighter seized by the neck and shattered into pieces. God has placed him in the open as a target for destruction.

Job pictures archers surrounding him and shooting arrows deep into his vital organs. His kidneys are pierced without mercy, and his gall bladder is spilled onto the earth like a fatal hunting blow. He feels mortally wounded by the trials piercing his body and soul.

Job describes himself as a stone city wall being smashed through breach after breach. God rushes upon him like an unstoppable warrior storming a broken fortress. Job has no strength left to hold back these overwhelming attacks.

Job says he has sewn scratchy sackcloth directly onto his skin as an ongoing mark of sorrow. He has pushed his horn, a common symbol of power and dignity, down into the dust. He is completely humbled and makes no attempt to hide his loss.

Job's face has turned red and swollen from constant weeping over his losses. Dark shadows ring his eyes as death seems to creep steadily closer. Unceasing grief has worn down both his spirit and his physical sight.

Job insists that he has not used violence or stolen from anyone to deserve such destruction. His prayers to God remain genuine, not the prayers of a hypocrite. He maintains his integrity before God even when circumstances look completely against him.

Job pleads with the earth not to hide his blood if he dies, comparing his suffering to an innocent person being murdered. In Scripture, unburied blood cries out to God until justice is done. Job wants his plea for justice to be heard until the truth about his innocence is revealed.

Job expresses a striking burst of faith, declaring that his true witness is in heaven. Even though his earthly friends condemn him, God above knows his innocence. Believers can rest in the truth that God sees their hearts when all human support fails.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching, citing Pope Gregory the Great, sees this verse as assurance that a believer with God as witness in heaven need not fear human judgment.

notes.meaning: Job watches his friends mock him instead of comforting him, so he turns his tear-filled eyes directly to God. Since humans will not listen, he pours out his broken heart to the Almighty. Taking our pain straight to God brings peace when earthly friends disappoint us.

Job wishes for someone to plead his case before God, just as a person argues for a neighbor in court. He longs for a fair hearing where his integrity can be vindicated. This cry reflects the human need for an advocate, which Christians see answered in Jesus Christ.

Job knows he has only a few numbered years left before he enters the realm of death. When he departs this world, he will not return to earthly life again. Facing the reality of death makes him long for his name to be cleared before his time is up.
